Average and marginal return by counterfactual simulation

Source: R/marginal-roi.R
marginal_roi.Rd

Computes a channel's average return and its marginal return by re-running the full media transform (carryover and saturation) on a counterfactually increased spend plan, rather than by differentiating the saturation curve at a single point. This is the definition of marginal ROI used in the Bayesian MMM literature (Jin et al., 2017) and in Google's Meridian: the incremental response from a small proportional increase in spend, divided by the incremental spend.

Usage

marginal_roi(
  spend,
  coefficient,
  adstock = list(kernel = "geometric", decay = 0.5),
  saturation = list(type = "none"),
  by = NULL,
  lift = 0.01,
  rows = NULL,
  extend = 0L,
  spec = NULL
)

Arguments

spend

Numeric vector of raw spend for one channel, in time order. Or a data frame with one row per period and a column of spend per channel, to compute every channel in one call. Spend must be complete, finite and non-negative.

coefficient

The channel's fitted coefficient on the transformed regressor. When spend is a data frame, a numeric vector of coefficients named by channel: coef(fit) will do with spec, but without spec every name is taken as a channel, so pass only the channels' coefficients.

adstock, saturation

Lists describing the transform, exactly as for media_transform(). They must match the transform the model was fitted on. When spend is a data frame and spec is NULL, every channel uses them.

by

Optional grouping vector, as for media_transform(), one element per element of spend. When spend is a data frame, one element or row per row, or column names of spend, as for transform_plan().

lift

Proportional increase in spend used for the marginal return. The default 0.01 asks what a 1% larger budget would have returned.

rows

Optional logical or integer index of the periods whose spend is increased (the planning window). Defaults to every period. Response is always summed over the whole series, so carryover from the window into later periods is counted.

extend

Number of zero-spend periods appended to the end of the series (to each group, when by is supplied) before summing response, so that carryover from late spend is allowed to play out. At most 1,000,000. The default 0 counts response only inside the observed window, as contributions() and roi() do, so the average return matches theirs. It also drops the carryover of late spend, which understates the marginal return of slow channels; see "Carryover after the window". Set it to effective_window() of the decay to measure long-run return.

spec

Optional list with one transform per channel, named by column, as for transform_plan(): each entry holds adstock and saturation, and optionally order. Only when spend is a data frame, and in place of adstock and saturation, which must then be left out. The channels are then the names of spec, and coefficient may hold other names, which are ignored. Without spec, the channels are the names of coefficient.

Value

A one-row data frame with columns spend (total spend over the series), contribution (the channel's total response), roi (their ratio, the average return) and mroi (incremental response per unit of incremental spend, when the spend in rows is increased by lift). A window with no spend is an error.

When spend is a data frame, one row per channel, in the order of spec or of coefficient, with a leading channel column and then the same columns. A channel with no spend in the window has an mroi of NA, and a message names it; with no spend at all, its roi is NA too.

Details

Differentiating the saturation curve, as mroi() does, answers a narrower question: the slope of the curve at one level of adstocked media. Turning it into a return on spend needs two further steps that are easy to get wrong.

  • Carryover. A unit spent this week enters this week's adstock with the kernel's first weight only (1 - decay for a normalised geometric kernel), but it also enters every later week's adstock. Under a normalised kernel those weights sum to one, so the total marginal return is close to the curve's slope, not to the slope times 1 - decay. Multiplying by the first weight gives the return inside the week of spend and ignores the rest; for a slow channel that understates its marginal return several-fold, and a reallocation driven by it moves money away from exactly the channels whose effect arrives late.

  • Averaging over periods. The curve's slope at the mean adstocked level is not the mean of its slope across periods. Flighted media spends some weeks near zero and some near saturation, and for an S-shaped curve the two can differ by a large factor (Jensen's inequality).

Simulation handles both by construction, for any kernel and any curve media_transform() supports, and it is what makes average and marginal return directly comparable: both are totals over the same periods.

Carryover after the window

With the default extend = 0, response that spend would produce after the last observed period is not counted. The loss falls on spend near the end of the window and grows with the decay. For mm_weekly's north television (decay 0.85) at its true parameters, the marginal return with extend = 0 is 1.084, about 4% below the 1.129 it reaches with extend = effective_window(0.85, 0.99); for search (decay 0.15) the difference is under 0.5%.

The default makes the average return here equal the one roi() reports from contributions(). For a budget decision, where each unit of spend should be credited with all the response it produces, pass extend = effective_window(decay, 0.99).

What this is not

The answer is only as good as the fitted curve, and a curve is identified only over the spend levels the data contains. A marginal return is a local quantity: a 1% change is the kind of question the data can speak to; a 50% change is extrapolation, which is why lift defaults to 0.01.

References

Jin, Y., Wang, Y., Sun, Y., Chan, D. and Koehler, J. (2017). Bayesian methods for media mix modeling with carryover and shape effects. Google Inc. https://research.google/pubs/pub46001/

See also

roi(), mroi(), response_curve(), media_transform(), simulate_plan(), allocate_budget()

Examples

data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

# Television: long carryover, S-shaped response
marginal_roi(
  north$tv, coefficient = truth$beta[["tv"]],
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[["tv"]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                    shape = truth$shape[["tv"]])
)
#>    spend contribution      roi     mroi
#> 1 266978     302361.4 1.132533 1.083959

# Letting the carryover from the final weeks play out
marginal_roi(
  north$tv, coefficient = truth$beta[["tv"]],
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[["tv"]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                    shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]),
  extend = effective_window(truth$decay[["tv"]], 0.99)
)
#>    spend contribution      roi     mroi
#> 1 266978     311695.6 1.167495 1.128674

# Only the last quarter's budget changes
last_q <- seq_len(nrow(north)) > nrow(north) - 13
marginal_roi(
  north$tv, coefficient = truth$beta[["tv"]],
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[["tv"]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                    shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]),
  rows = last_q
)
#>    spend contribution      roi      mroi
#> 1 266978     302361.4 1.132533 0.7083583

# Every channel in one call, each with its own transform
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
marginal_roi(north, truth$beta, spec = spec)
#>   channel  spend contribution      roi     mroi
#> 1      tv 266978    302361.38 1.132533 1.083959
#> 2   video  53248    130431.45 2.449509 1.522553
#> 3  search  74560    325735.31 4.368768 2.109446
#> 4  social  36716    105769.75 2.880753 1.665098
#> 5 display  26937     48394.19 1.796570 1.104525
